title: Cochabamba's water utility (SEMAPA) conceded to the Bechtel-led Aguas del Tunari
summary: On 3 September 1999 Bolivia's Water Superintendent signed a 40-year concession giving Aguas del Tunari, a consortium 55% owned through a Bechtel subsidiary, the right to run Cochabamba's water and sewer service, including a lease and transfer of the municipal utility SEMAPA's property. The concession took effect on 1 November 1999. After months of protests and a state of emergency, it was terminated in April 2000 and the service went back under public control. Aguas del Tunari filed an ICSID claim. In January 2006 the shareholders agreed to withdraw it with no compensation paid by either side, and ICSID recorded the discontinuance on 28 March 2006.

private.outcome: Concession terminated on 10 April 2000 after protests and a state of emergency; water service returned to public control under SEMAPA. Aguas del Tunari filed an ICSID claim (registered 25 February 2002), and the tribunal upheld its jurisdiction 2-1 in October 2005. In January 2006 the parties agreed that neither would pay compensation, and the case was discontinued on 28 March 2006. Reversed.

links.claim: Alongside the concession, the SEMAPA Property System Contract between Aguas del Tunari and SEMAPA provided for the commercial leasing and transfer of SEMAPA's property to Aguas del Tunari. Separate contracts leased the Misicuni tunnel and sold the Titiri pumping station to the concessionaire.

claims.claim: An IMF loan condition required Bolivia to privatize Cochabamba's water.
claims.explanation: The ESAF Policy Framework Paper of August 1998, prepared with IMF and World Bank staff, does list selling SEMAPA by December 1998 among the government's privatization plans. But the accompanying letter of intent of 14 August 1998 does not mention water or SEMAPA, and the paper does not show that SEMAPA's sale was a binding performance criterion. What actually happened in 1999 was a negotiated 40-year concession with a lone bidder, not a sale. PBS Frontline/World's timeline presents the sale as a condition of the IMF loan, which goes further than the IMF documents opened here.

claims.claim: The World Bank pushed the 1999 Bechtel water deal on Cochabamba.
claims.explanation: Advocacy groups and secondary accounts report that the Bank tied earlier water lending to privatizing the La Paz and Cochabamba utilities. They cite a 2002 World Bank evaluation précis that could not be opened for this record. PBS reports that a June 1999 Bank review said no subsidies should offset Cochabamba tariff rises. In a 2000 letter reproduced by the Democracy Center, however, the Bank said it had advised the government against the privatization plan and the tariff increases and had favored a different project. No primary document opened here shows that the Bank required the specific Aguas del Tunari contract.

claims.claim: Bolivia had to pay Bechtel compensation for cancelling the contract.
claims.explanation: Under the January 2006 settlement, neither the Government of Bolivia nor Aguas del Tunari paid compensation for the termination or for withdrawing the claim, and ICSID recorded the discontinuance on 28 March 2006 without any ruling on the merits.
